progressiveExplaining.eli5: Imagine a mailbox with a signal light on top. When you order a package, the signal light flips to 'Loading' and turns on the front porch waiting light (`<Suspense>`). When the package arrives, the signal holds the parcel and the waiting light turns off. If you ask for a different package, the mailbox fetches the new one and ignores any slow late packages from before.
progressiveExplaining.junior: `createResource` is Solid's built-in primitive for handling asynchronous data fetching. `const [data, { mutate, refetch }] = createResource(sourceSignal, fetcherFn);`. `data()` returns the fetched value, `data.loading` indicates active requests, and `data.error` captures failures. When used inside a `<Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>` boundary, Solid automatically suspends the boundary until the resource resolves.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, `createResource` integrates Promises with the synchronous reactive graph. When a source signal (e.g. `userId`) updates, `createResource` automatically cancels or discards stale in-flight requests using request ID tokens to prevent race conditions. If read inside a `<Suspense>` tracking scope while pending, it registers its pending promise with the nearest `SuspenseContext`, preventing downstream DOM nodes from mounting until resolution.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Under the hood, `createResource` creates a state signal holding the resolved data and an internal promise tracking slot. When the fetcher promise is pending, reading `data()` inside a reactive computation calls `SuspenseContext.increment()`. The Suspense boundary intercepts this, suppressing the main DOM branch and displaying the `fallback` branch. Upon promise resolution, the internal signal updates via `setResourceState` and triggers `SuspenseContext.decrement()`, switching to the resolved DOM tree.

codeComparison.title: Manual async/await Signal State vs createResource + Suspense
codeComparison.summary: Manual fetch orchestration causes race conditions and loading state boilerplate; `createResource` binds directly to Suspense.

legacyOrBad.label: Manual Fetch in createEffect
legacyOrBad.snippet: createEffect(async () => { setLoading(true); setData(await fetch()); }); // ❌ Race conditions

modernOrGood.label: createResource with Suspense
modernOrGood.snippet: const [user] = createResource(userId, fetchUser); // ✅ NEW: Auto-cancels stale requests & binds to Suspense

interviewGotchas.question: How does `createResource` prevent out-of-order response race conditions when the source signal changes rapidly?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your knowledge of asynchronous concurrency control in reactive systems.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: `createResource` maintains an internal monotonic sequence counter (request ID) for each fetch invocation. When the source signal updates (e.g. `userId` changes from 1 to 2), the sequence number increments. When an asynchronous fetch promise resolves, `createResource` checks if the resolved request ID matches the latest sequence counter. If an older request (user 1) resolves after a newer request (user 2), the older result is silently discarded.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Do not implement manual cancellation booleans inside custom fetchers; `createResource` handles stale response discarding automatically.

interviewGotchas.question: Can you read a resource outside of `<Suspense>` without crashing?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks knowledge of resource access semantics in non-suspense contexts.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Yes. If `data()` is read outside of a `<Suspense>` boundary, it will return `undefined` while pending (or its initial value if provided), and `data.loading` will return `true`. It will not throw or crash; it simply renders standard conditional checks (e.g. `{data() ? data().name : 'Loading...'}`).
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Using `data().name` without optional chaining or Suspense when `data()` is `undefined` will trigger a JavaScript `TypeError: Cannot read property of undefined`.
